For patients diagnosed with HIV, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should ideally be initiated at the time of diagnosis or within seven days. If this is not done, the reasons must be documented using specific codes. Re-engagement in HIV care should also be assessed, and any drug allergies, chronic conditions, or concurrent medications should be recorded. Tuberculosis (TB) status must be evaluated, including prior therapy, screening results, and treatment start dates. For HIV-exposed infants, follow-up care should include prophylactic medications, HIV testing, and determination of final HIV status. Interruptions in ART, such as missed doses or drug pick-ups, must be documented, including the reasons for the interruption and the date of restart if applicable. Follow-up status, including loss to follow-up, tracing efforts, or transfer to another facility, should also be recorded. For patients transferring in or out of care, the source or destination of transfer must be noted. At the initiation of ART, the clinical stage, CD4 count, and any coexisting conditions such as TB, hepatitis B (HBsAg+), hepatitis C (HCV RNA+), pregnancy, or breastfeeding status should be documented. Changes in ART regimens, whether due to toxicity, drug interactions, treatment failure, or other reasons, must be recorded with the corresponding dates and reasons for substitution or switching to secondor third-line therapies. For HIV care, baseline and ongoing assessments should include weight, height, nutritional status, and any comorbidities or coinfections. Vaccination status, TB screening, and hepatitis testing should be conducted as per national guidelines. Advanced HIV disease is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease. Functional status (working, ambulatory, or bedridden) should also be assessed for individuals with advanced HIV. Differentiated service delivery (DSD) models, such as fast-track ART refills or community-based ART groups, should be adapted to the patient’s needs. Eligibility for DSD includes being on ART for at least six months, having no current illness, demonstrating good adherence, and showing evidence of treatment success (e.g., suppressed viral load or adequate CD4 count). For patients with hepatitis, testing should be conducted at enrollment. If hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) or hepatitis C antibody (HCV Ab) is positive, further staging of liver disease should be performed, and treatment should be initiated as appropriate. Vaccination for hepatitis B should be provided to those who test negative. HIV-exposed infants require close monitoring, including prophylaxis, nutritional support, and HIV testing. Final HIV status should be determined, and any loss to follow-up or transfer of care should be documented. Nutritional counseling and support should be provided for both infants and older children, with specific attention to feeding practices and growth monitoring. Education and counseling for patients should cover basic HIV knowledge, prevention strategies (e.g., safer sex, partner testing, and prevention of mother-to-child transmission), and adherence to ART. Patients should be informed about managing side effects, what to do if a dose is missed, and how to maintain adherence during travel. Support systems, such as treatment supporters, should be identified and prepared to assist the patient. For TB, patients should be assessed at every visit for symptoms suggestive of TB, such as prolonged cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. If TB is suspected, appropriate diagnostic tests (e.g., smear, culture, or molecular WHO-approved rapid diagnostic tests) should be conducted, and results should be recorded. If TB is confirmed, treatment should be initiated, and the regimen documented. Preventive therapy for TB should be provided to those without active disease. Adverse drug reactions, including those limiting treatment, should be documented with specific details about the type of reaction (e.g., gastrointestinal, skin, neurological, or metabolic). For patients on ART, reasons for missed doses should be recorded, such as forgetting, side effects, travel, or stigma. Efforts should be made to address these barriers to adherence. Vaccination records for children should include all relevant immunizations, such as BCG, hepatitis B, polio, measles, and others as per national guidelines. For advanced HIV disease, additional screening tests, such as cryptococcal antigen or histoplasmosis antigen tests, may be required. In summary, comprehensive HIV care involves regular monitoring, timely initiation of ART, management of comorbidities, nutritional support, and patient education.
